description: Plain-language concepts the curriculum is built on. Each names the concepts it depends on and the lessons that teach it. Checked by tests/concepts.test.js.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.definition: Value is what something is worth to the person buying it, right now; a sale happens only when both sides gain.

explain.prompt: In your own words: why would a person pay KES 50 for something that cost the seller KES 15?

points.hint: It is worth more to the buyer than the money they pay
The seller gains too: they receive more than it cost
It is the right thing, in the right place or at the right moment

concepts.name: Revenue, cost and profit
concepts.definition: Profit is what is left of the money customers pay after the cost of the goods and the expenses of running the business.

explain.prompt: Explain the difference between a fixed and a variable cost, using a business you know.

points.hint: A variable cost changes with how much you sell
A fixed cost stays the same however much you sell
A real example, such as rent, a salary or ingredients

concepts.name: Percent
concepts.definition: A percent says what share one number is of another; it is only meaningful when you also know what it is a percent of.

explain.prompt: Why can two shops with the same average sale be very different businesses?

points.hint: The average hides how spread out the sales are
One shop may rely on a few huge sales, the other on many similar ones
An average alone does not tell you enough

concepts.name: Customer and problem
concepts.definition: A customer is someone with a problem they will pay to solve, and customers differ in who they are and how much they matter.

explain.prompt: Describe the customer for a business you might start: who are they, and what problem do they have, in their own words?

points.hint: Who the customer is
A problem they face
Why it matters to them, ideally in their own words

concepts.name: Price and margin
concepts.definition: A price sits between what it costs you and what it is worth to the customer; margin is the share of the price you keep.

explain.prompt: Explain the difference between margin and markup in your own words, with an example.

points.hint: Margin is measured against the price
Markup is measured against the cost
A number example

concepts.name: First principles
concepts.definition: Break a big question into parts that are certainly true and can be measured, then build the answer up from them.

explain.prompt: Take the question 'Should I start this business?' and break it into smaller questions you could answer with numbers.

points.hint: Customers: will enough people buy?
Profit: can it make money after its costs?
Cash: can I afford to start and last until customers pay?

concepts.name: Table
concepts.definition: A table is rows and columns: each row is one thing (a sale, a customer) and each column is one fact about it.

explain.prompt: What is the difference between a row and a column? Use the shop's customers as your example.

points.hint: A row is one thing, for example one customer
A column is one fact about every row, for example the town
Use both words, row and column

concepts.name: Filter
concepts.definition: Filtering keeps only the rows that meet a condition, so you look at the part of the data your question is about.

concepts.name: Aggregate
concepts.definition: Aggregating squeezes many rows into one number per group: a total, a count or an average for each customer, month or product.

concepts.name: Join
concepts.definition: A join lines up rows from two tables by a shared key, so facts kept in different places can be read together.

concepts.name: Data quality
concepts.definition: Data is only usable if you have checked what is in it: how many rows, what is missing, what is out of range.

concepts.name: Cleaning
concepts.definition: Cleaning means making the same thing look the same everywhere (one spelling, one date format) without losing information.

concepts.name: Duplicates
concepts.definition: A duplicate is the same real-world thing recorded twice; counting it twice makes every total wrong.

concepts.name: Reconcile
concepts.definition: Reconciling compares two records of the same facts (ledger and bank statement) and explains every difference.

concepts.name: Metric
concepts.definition: A metric is one agreed number that tracks how the business is doing, with a clear definition and a time period.

concepts.name: Unit economics
concepts.definition: Unit economics asks whether one sale, one customer or one product makes money after the costs it causes.

concepts.name: Margin
concepts.definition: Margin is what is left of the price after the cost of what you sold, shown as money and as a share of the price.

concepts.name: KPI
concepts.definition: A KPI is a metric chosen because a decision depends on it, shown with a target so people know when to act.

concepts.name: Average and spread
concepts.definition: An average says what is typical; the spread says how far real values stray from it. You need both to judge a number.

concepts.name: Trend
concepts.definition: A trend is the direction a number moves over time once the ups and downs of single periods are set aside.

concepts.name: Compare groups
concepts.definition: To say one group did better than another you must allow for chance, not only compare the two averages.

concepts.name: Stock
concepts.definition: Stock is money turned into goods: slow-moving or expiring stock ties up cash that cannot be used elsewhere.

concepts.name: Cash
concepts.definition: Cash is what is actually received and paid; a sale not yet paid for is profit on paper but not money in hand.

explain.prompt: A friend says 'I made a profit, so why is my account empty?' Give two reasons in plain language.

points.hint: Customers have not paid yet, because they bought on credit
The cash already went out for stock, bills or suppliers
Profit is what you earned; cash is what you actually hold

concepts.name: Investigate
concepts.definition: Investigating splits a change (profit fell) into its parts until you find which part moved and why.

concepts.name: Monitor
concepts.definition: Monitoring watches the numbers that matter, raises an alert at an agreed threshold, and records whether the action worked.

concepts.name: Real problem
concepts.definition: A problem worth solving happens often, hurts, and people already pay money or effort to cope with it.

explain.prompt: What three things make a problem worth solving, and how would you find out what people do about it today?

points.hint: It happens often
It hurts or costs something
People already pay or cope; ask them what they do today

concepts.name: Customer interview
concepts.definition: Ask about what people did and paid in the past, not whether they would buy in future, and count what you hear.

explain.prompt: Why is 'Would you buy this?' a weak question, and what would you ask instead?

points.hint: People are polite or poor at predicting
Ask about the past or present
Count or record what they say

concepts.name: Market size
concepts.definition: Size an opportunity bottom-up: reachable customers times the share who need it times what each pays.

explain.prompt: Why is '1 percent of the whole country' a weak way to size a business, and what do you do instead?

points.hint: It starts from a population not real people
Count customers you can reach
Multiply by share and price

concepts.name: Offer and price
concepts.definition: An offer says what the customer gets, for how much and by when, priced between your cost floor and the customer's value ceiling.

explain.prompt: What are the floor and the ceiling of a price, and why not price from cost alone?

points.hint: Floor is your cost plus needed profit
Ceiling is the value to the customer
Cost-only pricing leaves money on the table

concepts.name: Break-even
concepts.definition: Break-even sales equal fixed costs divided by the contribution each sale earns after its variable cost.

explain.prompt: What is the difference between a fixed and a variable cost, and how do they give a break-even number?

points.hint: Fixed costs stay the same
Variable costs rise with each sale
Fixed costs divided by contribution per sale

concepts.name: Runway
concepts.definition: Runway is how many months your cash lasts at the current monthly burn, which is why a profitable business can still run out of cash.

explain.prompt: What is runway, and why can a profitable business still run out of cash?

points.hint: Cash divided by monthly burn
Customers pay late while bills are due now
Profit is not cash

concepts.name: Conversion rate
concepts.definition: A conversion rate is the share of people at one step of the sales funnel who move to the next, such as visits to sales.

explain.prompt: What is a conversion rate, and what do you do with the reasons people say no?

points.hint: Share of people who move to the next step
Record the reasons for no
Learn and change the offer

concepts.name: Smallest version
concepts.definition: The smallest version gives a real customer the one result they pay for, often by hand, before anything is built.

explain.prompt: What is an MVP, and why start by doing the work by hand?

points.hint: The smallest thing that gives the result
Cheaper and fast to test whether people pay
Learn before building or scaling

concepts.name: Funding options
concepts.definition: Fund first with savings and sales, borrow only for something that earns more than the loan costs, and always confirm current terms.

explain.prompt: Why should a founder prefer savings and sales first, and what must a loan earn to be worth taking?

points.hint: Savings and sales carry no interest or ownership cost
A loan must earn more than it costs
Check current terms and total repayment

concepts.name: Registration, tax and contracts
concepts.definition: The law decides who may trade, who owes tax and who is bound by a promise, and the figures change, so confirm them at the official source.

explain.prompt: What are the three questions the law answers for a small business, and why must you check the figures yourself?

points.hint: Who may trade (registration)
Who owes tax or what is owed
Contracts or promises; figures change so check

concepts.name: Hiring
concepts.definition: A hire costs the salary plus the employer's statutory payments and should be made when the work is proven and the hire earns or saves more than they cost.

explain.prompt: Why is a salary not the true cost of an employee, and when should you hire?

points.hint: Employer pays extra contributions
Hire when work is proven
The hire must pay for themselves

concepts.name: Measure and iterate
concepts.definition: Track a few numbers each week, compare with last time, change one thing at a time and measure again.

explain.prompt: Why change only one thing at a time, and which three numbers would you track?

points.hint: Only one change shows the cause
Track a few key numbers
Measure, then repeat to avoid luck

concepts.name: Model and baseline
concepts.definition: A model is a rule that turns facts you have into a guess about something you do not, and it is only useful if it beats the simplest guess, the baseline.

explain.prompt: What is a model, what is the baseline, and why must a model beat the baseline?

points.hint: A model is a rule that turns known facts into a guess
The baseline is the simplest guess, such as always the average
A model that cannot beat the baseline has learned nothing useful

concepts.name: Train and test
concepts.definition: The data is split first: the model learns from the training set and is judged on the unseen test set, and anything from the test set leaking into learning makes the result dishonest.

explain.prompt: Why do we split data into a training set and a test set, and what is leakage?

points.hint: Learn from the training set, judge on the test set
The test must use data the model has never seen so it is honest
Leakage is when test information influences the learning

concepts.name: Fitting a line
concepts.definition: A fitted line predicts one number from another; its slope is how much the guess changes per unit of input, and it is computed from the training data only.

explain.prompt: What does the slope of a fitted line tell you, and why do we compute it from the training data only?

points.hint: The slope is how much the guess changes for each extra unit of input
The line is the best fit through the data, found from sums
Using the test data would be leakage so only training data is used

concepts.name: Error measures
concepts.definition: MAE is the average size of the miss, MSE squares the misses so large ones count far more, and the worst single miss shows an exception worth investigating.

explain.prompt: What is the difference between MAE and MSE, and why look at the worst miss?

points.hint: MAE is the average size of the miss
MSE squares the misses so big misses count much more
The worst miss shows an exception or an expensive failure

concepts.name: Classification and accuracy
concepts.definition: Predicting a category is classification; accuracy is the share right and it must beat the baseline of always guessing the most common category.

explain.prompt: What is the baseline for a yes or no prediction, and why can a model with high accuracy still be useless?

points.hint: The baseline always guesses the most common answer
Accuracy is the share of guesses that are right
High accuracy is useless if the baseline is already that high

concepts.name: Precision and recall
concepts.definition: Precision is how often a warning is right and recall is how many real cases it catches; they count the false alarms and the misses that one accuracy number hides.

explain.prompt: What are precision and recall, and why is accuracy alone not enough?

points.hint: Precision is how often a warning is right
Recall is how many of the real cases it catches
Accuracy hides the two kinds of mistake, which cost different amounts

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: A model that is far better on its training data than on new data has memorised noise instead of learning a pattern.

explain.prompt: What is overfitting and how do you spot it?

points.hint: The model memorises the training data and its noise instead of learning
You spot it by a big gap between the training score and the test score
It fails on new data it has not seen

concepts.name: Nearest neighbours
concepts.definition: Nearest neighbours predicts a new case from the average of the k most similar known cases; the distance measure and the size of k shape the result.

explain.prompt: How does nearest neighbours predict, and what do the distance measure and k change?

points.hint: It finds the most similar known cases
It averages what happened to those cases
The size of k and how distance is measured change the result

concepts.name: Features and leakage
concepts.definition: Features are the facts a model is given; a feature is only allowed if you would know it when you need the prediction, otherwise it leaks the answer.

explain.prompt: What is a feature, and what makes a feature leakage?

points.hint: A feature is a fact or input the model is given
Leakage is using something only known after the answer
It looks brilliant in testing but fails in real use

concepts.name: Language models
concepts.definition: A language model predicts the next piece of text, works in tokens that providers charge for, and can state false things confidently, so important answers are checked.

explain.prompt: What does a language model do, what is a token, and why can it be confident and wrong?

points.hint: It predicts the next piece of text
A token is a small piece of text that is counted and charged for
It can sound right and be wrong, so answers are checked

concepts.name: Retrieval and evaluation
concepts.definition: Retrieval searches your own documents for the passages that matter and gives them to the model; an evaluation set of questions with known relevant documents measures how well the search works.

explain.prompt: What is retrieval, and how do you know the search is working?

points.hint: Retrieval finds the relevant documents for a question
The found text is given to the model so it answers from it, not its memory
An evaluation set and recall measure the search

concepts.name: Drift and monitoring
concepts.definition: Drift is the data or behaviour moving away from what the model was built on; you decide in advance what to watch, what size of change triggers a check and who acts.

explain.prompt: What is drift, and what should you decide before a model goes live?

points.hint: Drift is the data changing from what the model was built on
Set a threshold that triggers a check
Decide in advance what to watch, who acts and keep versions

concepts.name: Data and types
concepts.definition: Everything is stored as bits; a type tells the computer how to read them as a number, text or date, and the type decides what you can do and how values sort.

explain.prompt: What is a data type, and why does it matter that 10 and 9 can sort differently?

points.hint: A type says how the stored bits are read (number, text, date)
Text sorts character by character, numbers by value, so the order differs
The type decides what you can calculate, so check it rather than assume

concepts.name: Files and formats
concepts.definition: CSV, Excel and JSON are three ways of writing the same table: lines of values, a workbook grid, or labelled records.

explain.prompt: How can one table be written as CSV and as JSON, and what does each give you?

points.hint: CSV is one row per line with values separated by commas
JSON writes each row as a record with the column name beside each value
They hold the same table, but formats differ in types, size and quoting

concepts.name: Tables and keys
concepts.definition: A table is rows (one thing each) and columns (one fact each); a key is a column that is different for every row and links tables.

explain.prompt: What are a row, a column and a key, and why is a name a poor key?

points.hint: A row is one thing and a column is one fact about every thing
A key is a value that is different for every row and identifies it
Names repeat or change, so an id is used and keys connect tables

concepts.name: Input, steps and output
concepts.definition: A program takes input, follows steps and gives output; its steps are made from variables, conditions and loops.

explain.prompt: What are the parts of a program, and what do a condition and a loop do?

points.hint: A program is input, steps and output
A condition chooses between paths depending on whether something is true
A loop repeats the same steps for each item

concepts.name: Why databases exist
concepts.definition: A database makes data shared, safe and fast; a transaction is a group of changes that all happen or none happen.

explain.prompt: Why do databases exist, and what is a transaction?

points.hint: Shared, many people use one copy
Safe: rules stop bad data and a failure does not lose it
A transaction is all changes together or none

concepts.name: Client, server, request, response
concepts.definition: A client sends a request to a server, which returns a response with a status code and usually data.

explain.prompt: Explain client, server, request and response, and what a 404 and a 500 mean.

points.hint: A client sends a request and a server sends a response
A 4xx code such as 404 means the request was wrong or not found
A 5xx code such as 500 means the server failed

concepts.name: Permissions, passwords and backups
concepts.definition: Give each person only the access the job needs, protect secrets, and keep a backup that you have tested by restoring it.

explain.prompt: What is least privilege, and why must a backup be tested?

points.hint: Least privilege means only the access the job needs
Backups must be restored to prove they work
Protect secrets with strong unique passwords and a manager, and security lowers risk but never removes it

concepts.name: Debugging as the scientific method
concepts.definition: State what you expected and what happened, form one hypothesis, run one test that could prove it wrong, and change one thing at a time.

explain.prompt: How is debugging like the scientific method, and why change one thing at a time?

points.hint: State what you expected and what actually happened
Form a hypothesis and run a test that could prove it wrong
Change one thing at a time so cause and effect stay clear

concepts.name: Auditing a messy source
concepts.definition: Measure a source you did not build, test one suspected cause at a time, clean a copy not the original, and report the effect in money.

explain.prompt: How would you audit a messy source before cleaning it, and why count again afterwards?

points.hint: Measure first: count rows and distinct values
Test a suspected cause, and clean a copy so the original is kept
Count again afterwards, and say what the problem cost

concepts.name: Cost at scale
concepts.definition: Work grows with the rows a query reads. Partitions, summary tables and incremental loads keep that number small as data grows.

explain.prompt: Why does a query's cost depend on the rows it reads, and how can you keep that number small as data grows?

points.hint: Cost follows the number of rows read
Partitions let a query skip the parts it does not need
Summary tables or incremental loads read less
